followUps:
Yes. A MAC address only has to be unique on its own local link, and in practice it is not guaranteed globally. Vendors burn in unique values, but VMs, containers and phones can use randomised or locally administered MACs, and cloning tools copy them.

Two devices on different LANs can share a MAC with no problem, because routers strip the Ethernet header at each hop. Two on the same LAN cannot: the switch would flip the entry between ports and frames would go to the wrong host.

Because MACs are flat and carry no location, so a router would need one entry per device in the world. Billions of devices means billions of entries, with no way to summarise them.

IP addresses are hierarchical: 10.1.2.0/24 covers 254 hosts in one route, and an ISP can announce one prefix for thousands of customers. A MAC such as aa:bb:cc:11:22:33 says only who made the card, not where it is. Moving a laptop to another network also keeps its MAC but needs a new IP that fits the new location.

Route aggregation (supernetting) means replacing many adjacent prefixes with one shorter prefix that covers them all, so neighbours see one route instead of many.

Example: 192.168.0.0/24, .1.0/24, .2.0/24, .3.0/24 are four routes. They share the first 22 bits, so they collapse to 192.168.0.0/22. The blocks must be contiguous and aligned to the power of two (4 blocks starting at a multiple of 4). This keeps the internet routing table smaller and hides churn inside the ISP.

RIPv1 did not send the mask in its updates, so it had to assume the classful mask from the address itself. That means it only supports one mask size per classful network and cannot carry VLSM or CIDR routes.

For example, it could not distinguish 10.1.1.0/24 from 10.1.1.0/26. RIPv2 added the mask (and multicast updates), which fixed this. It also forced discontiguous subnets of one class to be avoided, since summarisation happened at classful boundaries automatically.

code.title: Subnet calculator with bit operations
code.python:
# Subnet calculator with bit operations. O(1) time and space.
ip = (192 << 24) | (168 << 16) | (10 << 8) | 77
prefix = 26

def dotted(n):
    return ".".join(str((n >> s) & 255) for s in (24, 16, 8, 0))

mask = (0xFFFFFFFF << (32 - prefix)) & 0xFFFFFFFF  # prefix ones, then zeros
network = ip & mask                                # AND keeps the network bits
broadcast = network | (~mask & 0xFFFFFFFF)         # host bits all ones
hosts = 2 ** (32 - prefix) - 2                     # minus network and broadcast

print("Address:", dotted(ip) + "/" + str(prefix))
print("Mask:", dotted(mask))
print("Network:", dotted(network))
print("Broadcast:", dotted(broadcast))
print("First host:", dotted(network + 1))
print("Last host:", dotted(broadcast - 1))
print("Usable hosts:", hosts)

followUps:
A /27 has mask 255.255.255.224, block size 32, so 192.168.10.77 falls in the block starting at 64 (blocks: 0, 32, 64, 96...).

  • Network: 192.168.10.64
  • Broadcast: 192.168.10.95
  • Usable: .65 to .94
  • Hosts: 25 - 2 = 30

Each extra prefix bit halves the block, so the /26 block of 64 splits into two /27 blocks of 32.

No. With /26 the block size is 64, and .130 falls in the block starting at 128 (128 to 191), while .77 is in 64 to 127. The networks differ, so a host at .77 would send traffic to .130 via its default gateway.

Quick check: 130 AND 192 = 128, while 77 AND 192 = 64. Same subnet means both addresses give the same network after the AND with the mask. In the other direction, .130 is a valid host in 192.168.10.128/26 (usable .129 to .190).

code.title: Longest-prefix match on a small routing table
code.python:
# Longest-prefix match over a tiny routing table. O(R) per lookup here;
# real routers use tries or TCAM to make it fast.
import ipaddress

routes = [
    ("0.0.0.0/0", "ISP-gateway"),
    ("10.0.0.0/8", "core-A"),
    ("10.1.0.0/16", "core-B"),
    ("10.1.2.0/24", "branch-C"),
]
table = [(ipaddress.ip_network(p), hop) for p, hop in routes]

def lookup(dest):
    ip = ipaddress.ip_address(dest)
    matches = [(net, hop) for net, hop in table if ip in net]  # all matching entries
    net, hop = max(matches, key=lambda m: m[0].prefixlen)      # longest prefix wins
    return net, hop, len(matches)

for d in ["10.1.2.9", "10.1.9.9", "10.9.9.9", "8.8.8.8"]:
    net, hop, n = lookup(d)
    print(f"{d:10} matches {n} route(s), picks {net} via {hop}")

followUps:
Because the router must prefer the most specific route, and the prefix length tells you how specific it is. A metric only compares routes to the same destination, not routes of different sizes.

Example: 10.0.0.0/8 via ISP-A with metric 1 and 10.1.2.0/24 via a branch link with metric 100. A packet to 10.1.2.9 must go to the branch, because the /24 says that exact range lives there. If metric won, the branch would be unreachable. This is also how a more specific route (hijack or intentional exception) overrides a broad one.

A binary trie stores prefixes bit by bit, so a lookup walks at most 32 nodes (for IPv4) instead of comparing against every route. Cost: O(32), independent of the number of routes, versus O(R) for a linear scan.

While walking, you remember the last node that holds a route; when the next bit has no child, that remembered node is the longest match. Example: with 10/8 and 10.1/16 stored, looking up 10.1.5.5 passes the /8 node, then the /16 node, then falls off, and returns the /16. Path compression skips single-child chains to save memory and steps.

code.title: VLSM allocation, largest block first
code.python:
# VLSM: sort hosts descending, give each the smallest block that fits,
# and allocate sequentially so every block stays aligned. O(n log n).
import ipaddress

need = [60, 30, 12, 2]
print("Hosts needed:", need)
cursor = int(ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.1.0"))

for hosts in sorted(need, reverse=True):
    bits = 2                                  # host bits; block size 2**bits
    while 2 ** bits - 2 < hosts:              # usable = size - network - broadcast
        bits += 1
    size = 2 ** bits
    cursor = (cursor + size - 1) // size * size   # align to a multiple of size
    net = ipaddress.ip_network((cursor, 32 - bits))
    print(f"{hosts:3} hosts -> {net}  usable {size - 2}  "
          f"{net[1]} - {net[-2]}")
    cursor += size

print("Next free:", ipaddress.ip_address(cursor))

followUps:
You may waste space or fail to fit everything, because small blocks placed first break the alignment of the large ones. A block must start on a multiple of its own size.

Example: place the 2-host /30 at .0, then a /26 (64 addresses) cannot start at .4; the next valid start is .64, stranding .4 to .63 (60 addresses). Placing the /26 first at .0 and the rest after it leaves one clean free tail. Largest first keeps all the leftovers contiguous.

Yes, on a point-to-point link. RFC 3021 allows a /31 where both addresses are usable hosts, with no network or broadcast address. It saves 2 addresses per link: a /30 uses 4 for 2 hosts, a /31 uses 2.

Both ends must support it (modern routers and Linux do, some old gear does not). It is only for two-device links. For a LAN with three or more devices you still need a /29 or larger.

Gratuitous ARP is a host announcing its own IP-to-MAC mapping without being asked, sending an ARP request or reply where sender and target IP are the same address.

Uses: (1) detecting an IP conflict at boot (if someone answers, the address is taken), (2) updating neighbours' caches after a MAC change, and (3) failover: when a standby takes over a virtual IP (VRRP, keepalived), it sends a gratuitous ARP so switches and hosts learn the new MAC immediately instead of waiting for cache timeouts of a few minutes.

Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP), which runs on ICMPv6. Instead of broadcasting, a host sends a Neighbor Solicitation to the target's solicited-node multicast address (ff02::1:ffXX:XXXX, built from the last 24 bits of the target), and the target answers with a Neighbor Advertisement.

Only hosts sharing those last 24 bits hear it, so other machines are not interrupted, which is better than ARP's broadcast to everyone. NDP also handles router discovery and duplicate address detection.

So that all DHCP servers know which offer was chosen and can release the others. The client may have received offers from several servers.

If Request were unicast, only the chosen server would hear it, and the others would keep their offered address reserved until a timeout. As a broadcast, the Request includes the server identifier, so non-chosen servers withdraw. It must also be a broadcast because the client still has no IP address (source 0.0.0.0) and cannot get a unicast reply path until the Ack arrives.

DHCP snooping is a switch feature that blocks rogue DHCP servers. Ports are marked trusted (uplink to the real server) or untrusted (user ports); DHCP server messages such as Offer and Ack arriving on untrusted ports are dropped.

It also builds a binding table of MAC, IP, port and lease, which Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard use to stop ARP spoofing and address forgery. Without it, someone plugging in a home router could hand out a wrong gateway and capture traffic.

code.title: PAT table: private flows share one public IP
code.python:
# PAT/NAPT: many private hosts share one public IP via unique public ports.
PUBLIC_IP = "203.0.113.5"
next_port = 40000
out_map = {}   # (private ip, port, dest) -> public port
in_map = {}    # public port -> (private ip, port)

def outbound(src_ip, src_port, dest):
    global next_port
    key = (src_ip, src_port, dest)
    if key not in out_map:                    # new flow: allocate a unique port
        out_map[key] = next_port
        in_map[next_port] = (src_ip, src_port)
        next_port += 1
    return f"{PUBLIC_IP}:{out_map[key]}"

def inbound(public_port):
    if public_port in in_map:                 # reply: rewrite back to private
        ip, port = in_map[public_port]
        return f"deliver to {ip}:{port}"
    return "drop (no mapping)"

print("10.0.0.2:5000 -> web  becomes", outbound("10.0.0.2", 5000, "198.51.100.7:443"))
print("10.0.0.3:5000 -> web  becomes", outbound("10.0.0.3", 5000, "198.51.100.7:443"))
print("10.0.0.2:5000 -> web  again   ", outbound("10.0.0.2", 5000, "198.51.100.7:443"))
print("reply to port 40001:", inbound(40001))
print("unsolicited to port 22:", inbound(22))

followUps:
Full cone and symmetric are two NAT mapping behaviours that decide whether outsiders can reach a host through an existing mapping.

  • Full cone: once 10.0.0.2:5000 maps to 203.0.113.5:40000, any external host can send to that public port and be forwarded. Easiest for peer-to-peer.
  • Symmetric: a new public port is used for each destination, and only that destination may reply. Hole punching with STUN usually fails, so apps fall back to a TURN relay.

Restricted and port-restricted cone sit in between, filtering by source IP or IP and port.

No, not by design. NAT is an address-sharing trick. It happens to block unsolicited inbound connections because no mapping exists, but that is a side effect, not a security control.

It does not stop malware that connects outward, does not inspect traffic, and can be bypassed by port forwarding, UPnP or hole punching. A stateful firewall provides the real protection, and IPv6 networks without NAT are protected the same way, by a default-deny inbound firewall rule.

It is the problem where bad news travels slowly in distance-vector routing, so routers keep increasing the cost to an unreachable network until they hit the maximum.

Example: A reaches net X via B at cost 2. B loses X. Before B learns that, A advertises 'X at 2'; B thinks X is reachable via A at cost 3; then A updates to 4, B to 5, and so on, looping packets until RIP's limit of 16 (infinity). Fixes: split horizon (do not advertise a route back out the interface it came from), poison reverse, hold-down timers and a small maximum metric.

An OSPF area is a group of routers that share the same detailed link-state database, which limits how far flooding and SPF calculations reach in a big network.

Area 0 is the backbone; every other area connects to it through area border routers (ABRs), which summarise routes between areas instead of passing every link. A link flap inside area 5 only triggers SPF runs on routers in area 5, not on thousands elsewhere. This reduces memory, CPU and convergence time.

code.title: Shorten and expand IPv6 addresses

followUps:
Because SLAAC builds the address from the 64-bit prefix plus a 64-bit interface identifier, so the split between network and host must sit exactly at bit 64.

A 64-bit host part is also what makes a random identifier (for privacy) collision-resistant, and many features assume it: Neighbor Discovery, SEND, and hardware tables. A /64 holds 264 addresses, far more than any LAN needs. Using a /120 on a point-to-point link works technically but breaks SLAAC and is discouraged for ordinary LANs.

Privacy extensions (RFC 4941) make a host use temporary, randomly generated interface IDs instead of one derived from its MAC address, so you cannot be tracked across networks by a fixed identifier.

The host keeps a stable address for incoming connections (or a stable-privacy one) and generates a fresh temporary address for outgoing connections, usually rotating it every day or so. Old addresses stay valid until existing connections finish. Example: 2001:db8:1:2:a1b2:c3d4:e5f6:1234 today, a different last 64 bits tomorrow.

The surprise costs are data processing charges and cross-AZ traffic, not just the hourly price. An AWS NAT gateway costs money every hour plus a per-GB fee for all data it processes.

  • Pulling large container images or S3 data through NAT: use gateway or interface VPC endpoints instead.
  • One NAT per AZ doubles hourly cost, but routing through a NAT in another AZ adds cross-AZ transfer charges.
  • Idle gateways in dev environments still bill hourly.

Example: 10 TB a month at about 4.5 cents/GB is roughly 450 USD in processing fees alone, so measure with flow logs.

Do not open the private subnet. Put a controlled entry point in front of the service and let the partner reach only that. Options: a public or internal load balancer with security-group or WAF rules limited to the partner's IP range, an API gateway with authentication, a PrivateLink endpoint service, or a site-to-site VPN.

Example: partner IPs allow-listed on an NLB in a public subnet, forwarding to targets in the private subnet, with mutual TLS on top. The service itself stays unreachable except through that path.

IPAM (IP address management) keeps one central record of every allocated range, and new VPCs get their CIDR from it instead of being picked by hand, so ranges are never reused.

Example: a company plan gives each region a /12 from 10.0.0.0/8, and each VPC a /16 from that pool; the tool refuses a request that overlaps an existing block. Tools like AWS VPC IPAM can also scan for overlaps and be checked in CI. The bug is prevented when the ranges are chosen, not found later when two networks need to connect.

PrivateLink exposes a single service, not the network. The provider publishes an endpoint service behind a Network Load Balancer, and the consumer creates an interface endpoint in its own VPC that gets a private IP from the consumer's own range.

Traffic is one-way (consumer to provider), uses only the listed ports, and the provider never sees the consumer's CIDR beyond translated addresses. That is why overlapping CIDRs do not matter: there is no route between the VPCs at all, only that one endpoint.

A hierarchical FIB stores next hops in a shared table and has prefixes point to an entry in it, so one update fixes many prefixes at once.

Example: 500,000 BGP prefixes all use the same next hop (peer P). If P's link fails, a flat FIB rewrites 500,000 entries one at a time, which can take seconds of blackholing. With a hierarchy, the router changes one next-hop object from P to a backup and all 500,000 prefixes follow immediately. This is the idea behind BGP PIC (prefix independent convergence).

LPM first picks the single best prefix, and ECMP then spreads traffic among the equal-cost next hops of that one winning route. They are separate steps: ECMP never mixes next hops from different prefix lengths.

The router hashes flow fields (source and destination IP, ports, protocol) and uses the hash to choose one of the N next hops, so packets of one flow stay in order on the same path. Example: 10.1.0.0/16 has 4 equal paths; hash mod 4 picks one per flow.

464XLAT lets IPv4-only apps work on an IPv6-only mobile network. The phone's CLAT translates IPv4 packets to IPv6 (stateless NAT46), and the carrier's PLAT translates them back to IPv4 (stateful NAT64) towards the internet.

An app opens a socket to a hard-coded IPv4 address such as 198.51.100.10; the CLAT wraps it into an IPv6 packet inside the carrier prefix, the network carries it over IPv6, and the PLAT turns it back to IPv4 using a shared public address. Native IPv6 traffic skips all of this.

Because RFC 1918 defines the private ranges for use inside one customer network. 100.64.0.0/10 (RFC 6598) is a separate shared address space meant only between a carrier and its customers.

If the ISP used 10.x or 192.168.x for its inside network, it would clash with the customer's home LAN using the same range, and routing would break. A dedicated range avoids the overlap. It is not globally routable, so it must not appear on the public internet, and customers should not use it on their own LANs either.

It means basic IP routing and the link work, but name resolution is broken, which is a DNS problem, not a routing problem.

Test: ping 8.8.8.8 succeeds, ping google.com says 'unknown host'. Check /etc/resolv.conf or resolvectl status, try dig @8.8.8.8 google.com to bypass the configured resolver, and check whether DHCP gave a DNS server. If direct queries work, the configured DNS server is wrong or unreachable.

MTU trouble looks like: small things work (ping, DNS, TCP handshakes) but large transfers hang or stall. Pages half load, SSH logs in and then freezes on a big output, TLS handshakes fail when the certificate packet is big.

Cause: a path link with a smaller MTU (for example a VPN or PPPoE at 1492 or 1400) while ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages are blocked, so the sender never learns to shrink packets. Test with ping -M do -s 1472 host and lower the size until it passes. Fix with MSS clamping or a smaller interface MTU.
